title: Mathios Arkangelo killing: Community leaders dismayed after officer who shot man returns to active duty
subtitle: Edmonton police confirmed Wednesday that the unidentified officer has completed a "reintegration" program following the deadly shooting "and has returned to active duty"
article: Leaders in Edmonton's Black and African communities say they're frustrated after learning the police officer who shot Mathios Arkangelo has resumed work.
Edmonton police confirmed Wednesday that the unidentified officer has completed a "reintegration" program following the deadly shooting "and has returned to active duty."
EPS spokeswoman Cheryl Sheppard acknowledged the " tragedy of this incident" but urged family and community members to trust the independent investigation process.

"While the EPS would like to share more information with the public about our police response on June 29, 2024, we have no choice but to respect the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team's (ASIRT) process," she said.

"While we cannot comment on the substance of this incident at this time, we are confident that ASIRT will be conducting a thorough and independent investigation which the EPS will fully co-operate with. We trust that those who advocate for effective oversight for policing will also respect the system and process set up to do so."
The statement comes days after community groups called for the officer to be suspended during the ASIRT probe.

Funke Olokude, president of the Nigerian Canadian Association of Edmonton, issued a joint statement Tuesday with the Nigerian Leadership Circle, saying youth in Edmonton's African, Caribbean and Black communities are "feeling frightened and uncertain about their safety" after seeing video of Arkangelo's death.
Arkangelo's family wants the officer suspended during the investigation "to maintain the integrity of the process and ensure public trust of the administration of justice," the statement said.
"Furthermore, we see it as crucial to protect the public from this unidentified officer."
Olokude called the decision "disheartening."

"The community's call for clarity and understanding has gone largely unanswered," she said. "This has the potential of affecting the community's trust in the Edmonton police, viewing the decision as a lack of accountability, especially as the circumstances of Mathios' death currently in the community are contentious and perceived as unjust."
The groups also called for expedited release of the autopsy report, as well as a "prompt and thorough" ASIRT investigation.

Arkangelo, 28, died after an officer shot him June 29. In a preliminary news release, ASIRT said police were called after reports of a single vehicle rollover on Anthony Henday Drive. The driver was found on foot in the nearby community of Fraser, where a patrol officer confronted him.
The day after the shooting, Edmonton police said the crash involved an impaired driver, though ASIRT's July 9 release did not make that claim.

Surveillance footage released by Arkangelo's family shows the lone officer arriving and confronting Arkangelo from more than a vehicle length away. Arkangelo reaches into his pocket for a utility knife, which he opens and holds out with both arms extended.

On June 29th, 2024, the Edmonton Police Service shot and killed Mathios Arkangelo, a 28-year-old Black youth from the South-Sudanese community. Despite him having raised his hands and surrendering, he was still gunned down multiple times. Viewer discretion is advisedbut here... pic.twitter.com/CtIiGS5mk1
The family said they do not know why Arkangelo did so, but said he used the knife for work and may have been trying to show the officer he wasn't hiding a weapon.

The officer unholsters his pistol and, moments later, fires at Arkangelo. After one of the shots, Arkangelo drops the knife. He looks down at the blood forming on his shirt, then lowers himself to the ground and collapses on his back.

Tom Engel, the family's lawyer, said based on audio from the surveillance videos, the officer fired four shots, but it is unclear how many hit Arkangelo. There appears to have been a delay in providing first aid, he said, noting it appears police initially handcuffed Arkangelo after he was shot.
Dunia Nur, president of the African Canadian Civic Engagement Council, called the officer's return to work "deeply troubling."
"It's a significant breach of public confidence, especially for communities like ours that disproportionately die or are victims of police violence."
She said there are similarities with the case to that of Sammy Yatim, who was shot to death by a Toronto police officer while carrying a knife on a streetcar.
The officer in that case, James Forcillo, was quickly suspended and was charged by Ontario's police watchdog within months. When he initially returned to work , it was in an administrative capacity.
"That is the minimum of what accountability should look like here in Edmonton," Nur said.

The EPS reintegration program is a "streamlined, peer-driven" return-to-work program for officers involved in "critical" incidents including shootings, Sheppard said. It includes both short- and long-term programs that aim to "diminish the potential for long-term psychological injury." The long-term program includes clinical care, peer support and traditional police training, she said.
